sections.heading_text: How do we safely grant autonomy to commodity intelligence?
sections.topic_sentence: This is a book about engineering: what engineering becomes when reasoning capacity is abundant.
*Agentic engineering* is the engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work.

One way to understand MAGE is as a classical software-engineering move: **add a level of indirection.**[^indirection] Conventional engineering has long separated the engineering of an artifact from its physical realization.
MAGE grew out of an engineering problem I encountered while building DocAble, a service for making documents accessible to people with disabilities.
This book is for software engineers who want to understand what changes when implementation can be delegated to capable agents.
**Authority.** Who is entitled to exercise engineering judgment: to decide what a system must do, permit or refuse an action, and answer for the result?
**Agent.** An AI system that pursues an open-ended or underspecified task through multiple steps, exercising judgment about what to do next and using tools in response to intermediate results.
**Agentic engineering.** The engineering of systems and environments in which autonomous agents perform consequential work.

preamble_points.text: Coding agents make software implementation cheap enough to change the engineering problem, creating the question of what engineers should do with the new productive capacity.
A printer can produce many kinds of artifacts, subject to the capabilities and limitations of its machinery.
People make broad productive capacity useful by developing forms and ways of working.
Software agents supply broad productive capacity and can infer implementation decisions that incomplete instructions leave unspecified.
Delegation can leave useful judgment to the agent, but the engineer decides which decisions to make explicit and which to delegate.

sections.heading_text: Consequential Choices and Degrees of Freedom
sections.topic_sentence: Delegating implementation is useful only if we can avoid doing much of the implementation work ourselves.

points.text: Even a simple software specification leaves enormous freedom — ten lines or ten thousand, a monolith or microservices — so engineers can specify the properties that matter and leave other decisions to the intelligence performing the work; which choices can safely remain open is itself an engineering decision.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineers can externalize those decisions by shaping the environment in which agents work.

points.text: As implementation becomes abundant, engineering leverage moves toward the instructions, representations, constraints, evidence, and infrastructure that shape autonomous work.
A governed engineering environment carries engineering decisions forward by making consequential knowledge available, enforcing selected obligations, and preserving evidence for control.

sections.heading_text: When Agents Produce the Wrong Result
sections.topic_sentence: “’Tis a poor craftsman who blames his tools.” A 3D-printed bracket may fail because the printer lacks the required accuracy, but also because its design or fabrication instructions were unsuitable.

points.text: Before blaming productive machinery, examine the engineer’s work in representing the problem, choosing required properties, and arranging how the result will be checked.

Agent inference can fill gaps in the engineering supplied to it, hiding omissions; a completed artifact does not establish that the inferred choices satisfy the intended properties or acceptable tradeoffs.
Inspect the instructions, problem representation, task boundary, tools, and required evidence before diagnosing a capability limit; failed output alone does not establish that limit.
Abundant implementation raises the stakes: capable agents execute a bad direction at extraordinary speed, and velocity amplifies sound engineering and bad engineering alike.

sections.topic_sentence: In 2024, the U.S.

points.text: University document accessibility combines an explicit legal obligation, semantic and structural requirements, and institutional scale.
DocAble's requirements include genuine accessibility, preservation, accountability, and practical operation at scale.

sections.topic_sentence: Purdue had licensed tools that could identify accessibility problems in course materials, but they did not fix them.

points.text: One project answered both problems: build the accessibility system, and use the engineering work to discover what sustained agentic development demanded.
The user supplies an inaccessible document and receives a remediated document and a changelog.
Art, language instruction, and handwritten mathematics illustrate why accessible output depends on the document's educational purpose.
Semantic interpretation helps propose changes; reliable document processing and suitable evidence are needed to establish whether the result satisfies the obligations.

preamble_points.text: MAGE emerged from developing and studying DocAble; the case introduces the engineering experience behind the methodology.

sections.heading_text: Foundation Models: The Source of Commodity Intelligence
sections.topic_sentence: The coding agents available in 2026 are built primarily around large language models (LLMs), which serve as their **foundation models**.

points.text: Coding agents combine capabilities acquired through foundation-model training with harness facilities that turn responses into action; engineers can shape their operating environment without changing trained weights.

sections.topic_sentence: Four properties of contemporary foundation models matter to the engineering argument.

points.text: Four properties of contemporary foundation models matter to engineering: broad semantic reasoning supports delegated implementation, probabilistic output calls for independent assurance, bounded working state motivates external representations, and inexpensive repeated reasoning increases the need for scalable governance.

The reasoning horizon is the practical limit of work the reasoner and its supporting machinery can carry through reliably, given the available representations and resources; task demands are distinct from this system-level limit.
Natural-language requests can leave consequential choices implicit, and iterative changes can lose earlier obligations; FlowCheck provides a concrete scheduler example.

sections.topic_sentence: A foundation model supplies general reasoning capabilities, but the effectiveness of an agent also depends on how its harness organizes the work.

points.text: The harness supplies action through tools, context management, and interposition; it may also support task management and parallel execution.

sections.heading_text: A Simple Probabilistic Model of Success with Agents
sections.topic_sentence: An agent may be highly reliable on individual tasks.

points.text: Decisions that depend on agentic inference form the probabilistic surface; mechanisms can enforce particular requirements even when the agent makes a mistake.

preamble_points.text: The roles of the model, harness, and environment explain where engineers can exercise control.

The reasoning horizon grounds the Representation Problem: explicit representations can reduce task-state and reconstruction demands, and Modeling addresses how to preserve the properties relevant to an engineering question.

The Enforcement Problem asks how important obligations can bind autonomous work without relying on the agent remembering or self-certifying each time; Alignment addresses this problem alongside the Representation Problem already named at the reasoning horizon.

Modeling makes consequential properties explicit and can reduce reconstruction or support assurance; Alignment connects selected obligations to mechanisms that restrict agents’ actions and determine whether work may be accepted. Modeling can improve the information supplied to an agent, while Alignment can improve feedback and prevent acceptance of violations within the enforcing mechanism’s scope.

The engineering questions extend beyond software, while useful representations, credible evidence, and the appropriate balance of delegation and governance depend on the domain. The following chapters develop the mechanisms, practice, evidence, theory, and wider implications.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineering models can describe a system, its environment, or the relationship between them.

points.text: The engineering question determines which relationships within the system, its environment, or between them matter.
Scope identifies what the model represents; assumptions identify the conditions under which an analysis applies.
An authoritative model states which properties a change must preserve; a descriptive model can record a current choice without making it a requirement.

sections.topic_sentence: A **model** is a purposeful reduction of a system.

points.text: A model is a purposeful reduction; its value is what it leaves out. The engineering question decides what to keep.

sections.topic_sentence: Choosing a model also means choosing its granularity: how much detail should it contain?

points.text: Omitting a service boundary can hide a prohibited call, while including every internal dependency can obscure the boundary being examined.

sections.topic_sentence: A model is not the system it represents.

points.text: Obligations rarely fix one implementation; a tolerance bounds permitted variation, a degree of freedom is a choice left open.
Preserving a degree of freedom defers a decision to a reasoner better positioned to make it: information may arrive later, and the implementing agent can acquire evidence before deciding.

sections.topic_sentence: An engineering model may establish the obligations without providing enough guidance for a particular implementer to satisfy them.

points.text: The engineering problem sets the obligations regardless of the implementer; a more capable human or agent may need less scaffolding but still needs the relevant information in the model or from other evidence.
A tacit obligation can look free; the "not that" test reveals a boundary that was never written down.
A model earns its place by the question it settles, not by how much of the system it represents.

sections.heading_text: Models Are Not a Silver Bullet
sections.topic_sentence: Modeling is not a silver bullet, to borrow Brooks’s phrase [cite: brooks1987].

preamble_points.text: Preserving project knowledge across tasks reduces repeated reconstruction.

Natural language is a representation, and often an appropriate one; consequential knowledge kept only in prose must be articulated correctly and then recovered correctly by each later reasoner, and a structured model can preserve distinctions that would otherwise be restated or reconstructed.
Modeling is not new: engineering has long used representations that suppress irrelevant detail so a property can be reasoned about directly.

sections.topic_sentence: The engineer’s role is to identify the engineering question and select a model that makes it easier to answer.

points.text: Software engineers need not invent a representation from first principles each time; engineering fields have accumulated a large repertoire of models for recurring questions, each preserving different information and supporting different analyses.
The practical skill is recognizing the engineering question and selecting a representation that preserves the properties needed to answer it; MAGE prescribes no new notation.

This chapter illustrates modeling practice rather than exhausting it; once the engineering question is known, start with the representations the field has already developed — the repertoire is reusable engineering knowledge, and choosing from it remains engineering judgment.
What matters is not a representation's graphical shape but the engineering question its entities and relations preserve.
Shape does not distinguish representations, semantics do; semantic commitment decides how much of that meaning is declared rather than understood.

sections.topic_sentence: Engineering models range from whiteboard sketches to specifications written in a programming language.

points.text: A representation can preserve the right distinctions while its interpreters supply most of its meaning.
Explicit semantics preserve meanings that later agents would otherwise have to infer without the shared context of the original team.
Semantic commitment: how much meaning the representation itself carries explicitly.
Purposeful reduction determines which distinctions to preserve; semantic commitment determines how precisely the representation defines them.
Semantic precision and generative completeness are different properties.
Stronger semantics buy capabilities and create obligations; they are not inherently better.
Concrete artifacts illustrate the range; the rows are examples, not maturity levels.
Stronger commitment aids mechanical interpretation; it moves interpretation burden rather than removing it.
An explicit transition relation allows a path property to be checked; composing machines also requires a choice of communication semantics.

sections.topic_sentence: Models can be maintained in ordinary project files, databases, or specialized modeling environments.

points.text: Structure — an explicit declared shape a machine can read — is what lets a representation be traversed, checked, and joined.
The simplest useful form of externalized knowledge is a graph of engineering entities and their relations; graph names the structure, not the storage.
Increasing semantic commitment can make additional capabilities possible — not a required sequence or maturity model.

sections.topic_sentence: [ref:question-to-consequence-progression] follows an engineering question from model selection through analysis to a decision.

points.text: Validation examines whether the model represents the distinctions, assumptions, and behaviors needed for the question.
A model's semantics determine which analyses can produce evidence for a design decision. Implementation conformance requires separate evidence.

preamble_points.text: An exploratory implementation can expose constraints, tradeoffs, state distinctions, dependencies, and bounds that were not evident in the initial design.
The agent may supply a design insight; the engineer takes responsibility for adopting it by evaluating it against the system's requirements.
Models support engineering design, direct agent work, and supply properties against which results can be checked.
Implementing and trying a design can reveal distinctions that were not evident in the initial model.

Neither direction guarantees the boundary is right; analysis, implementation, measurement, or failure may reveal that an omitted distinction mattered or an included one did not, and the model is revised when the evidence changes the engineering judgment.

sections.topic_sentence: We will examine each class of model in the same way.
Consider a web application with an API, a cache, and a database.

points.text: The architectural question selects components and their permitted direct dependencies.
Removing API and searching for a remaining Web-to-Database path tests whether the declared architecture permits a bypass.

sections.topic_sentence: Structural models support several kinds of questions about how a system is organized.
DocAble is a service that repairs accessibility problems in documents, such as missing alternative text, unmarked table headers, or incorrect reading order.
DocAble supports several document formats through libraries powerful enough to alter their underlying structures.

points.text: The model draws one architectural relation — remediation reaches format-specific mutation through a structured-document seam, implemented per format — and leaves queues, retries, sessions, and repair mechanics out.

The model states the path requirement that ordinary mutation routes cross the structured-document seam; DocAble protects the boundary using format-specific static restrictions and runtime write-authority checks.

A structural model can become stale as implementation changes — the code moves and the drawing does not — so the boundary it shows quietly stops matching the system; that gap is model drift, and later sections keep the correspondence by deriving, generating, or tracing.

sections.heading_text: What computations depend on one another?
sections.topic_sentence: The document-mutation model identifies where changes belong.

points.text: A second structural question reaches inside remediation: which computations make up the pipeline, and how do they depend on one another; the first reduction treats each registered pass as a node.

DocAble's computation model represents registered computations as nodes and distinguishes a data-flow edge (information consumed to produce a result) from a control edge (information consulted only to decide whether to run).

The same model records each computation's mutation behavior — read-only, a typed patch for all or part of its edits, or a direct in-place edit — exposing distinctions the implementation contains but does not represent uniformly.

The computation model is static per run, but other views attach observations to its stable computation identities — DocAble joins staged-run latency and cost to those identities without turning the structural graph into an execution log.

Additional engineering views attach by computation identity rather than enlarging the structural schema; declared properties state intent, measured properties report observation, so an unmeasured value is unknown, not zero.
The document-mutation model locates architectural bypasses; the computation model supports change-impact analysis through data and control dependencies.

sections.topic_sentence: As with structural models, we begin with a small example, then examine the properties and analyses it supports before turning to DocAble.
A service processes jobs that may be waiting, running, completed, or failed.

points.text: Reducing a service to states and transitions turns "can it reach a state it should never occupy?" from a reconstruction over scattered handlers into a question a person or tool can answer.

A partial transition function defines the effects of start, finish, and fail in a four-state job lifecycle. Undefined pairs admit no transition, and the same function can guide implementation, interpretation, or test generation.

sections.topic_sentence: Behavioral models let us investigate which states a system can reach, which sequences of events are permitted, and whether required outcomes eventually occur.

points.text: A behavioral model represents states and transitions; it can specify allowed behavior or describe behavior to be checked against a requirement. Safety and liveness properties ask different questions over the admitted executions.

State-transition models make lifecycle and recovery questions explicit; state machines, labeled transition systems, and statecharts represent behavior, while temporal specifications state properties over executions.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble distributes document accessibility work across workers that may fail or lose their assignments.
A worker recovering a document job may have a corrected artifact available locally before uploading it to persistent storage.

points.text: The recovery obligation lives in the gap between local staging and durable publication: there is no direct FALLBACK_STAGED to DB_UPDATED edge, so the model excludes executions in which the record points at a not-yet-durable artifact.
The recovery model keeps the states needed to check publication order; a fuller job lifecycle can support broader workflow questions when it includes the relevant transitions.

sections.heading_text: Distinguishing a current owner from a returning one
sections.topic_sentence: DocAble leases each in-flight job to one worker.

points.text: Concurrent workers can acquire, lose, and regain rights to a job; locks, leases, capabilities, and claims express different aspects of access and ownership, which the model selects according to the question.

A job is leased exactly when it has an owner; the two are the same fact from two sides, so the model represents ownership as the presence of a current claim — this is what "leased" means, and it sets up the invariant that follows.

Suppose A holds generation 7, stalls, and is reclaimed; the job is re-leased to B at generation 8; a late release from A carrying generation 7 must not clear B's generation-8 claim, and the generation makes that decidable.

A claim binds a holder to a resource and carries which holder, which generation of claim, and when it expires — the generation being what tells a current claim from a superseded one — and because the hard failures live in interleavings, the characteristic analysis is state-space exploration with invariant checking.
The model omits processing topology while preserving ownership, generation, lifetime, and reclamation; a changed implementation must be checked for correspondence with those semantics.

Read as ownership the lease says who controls a job; read as behavioral it traces a claimed-held-expired-reclaimed lifecycle; counted, it measures how much work is in flight — one representation, three questions.

The overlap follows from the distinction introduced at the chapter's opening: model classes identify engineering questions, not mutually exclusive data structures — the observation the closing section builds on to connect the models.

sections.topic_sentence: We will again begin with a small example, examine the properties and analyses it supports, and then turn to DocAble.
A service sells prepaid credits and also offers unlimited subscriptions.

points.text: Decision tables, rule systems, and constraint systems make choices explicit; policy is one kind of decision model, expressed through access-control matrices, policy graphs, and feature models as well as those general forms.

An observed-call edge and a permitted-call edge can look identical while answering different questions; in the illustrated models, a missing edge means no recorded call or no permitted call respectively.
An image's informational role depends on context; DocAble uses a VLM classification with an explicit conservative policy that retains content when the classification is uncertain.

sections.topic_sentence: Decision models let us examine whether the available rules cover the cases they must handle, whether those rules agree, and whether the choices they permit satisfy the applicable constraints.

points.text: Once permission is declared, the claims a policy designer wants become expressible — permitted/forbidden, mutual exclusion, prerequisites, consistency, completeness, least privilege — and "is this allowed?" becomes an evaluation rather than an argument.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble uses decision models for several purposes: deciding whether an image needs a description, declaring which services may communicate, and determining whether a user may upload a document.
Accessibility remediation must distinguish images that convey information from those that are merely decorative.
DocAble distributes document remediation across several services.

points.text: The typed graph declares permitted inter-service edges and is checked against the dependency map consumed by deployment; completeness checks concern the declaration, while runtime permission depends on installed controls.

DocAble checks the typed graph against the deployment dependency map but does not reconcile observed traffic against it at runtime; whether the deployed services stay on the permitted edges, and what a departure should cost, is Alignment's question.

sections.topic_sentence: The service-flow model determines which calls are permitted.

points.text: The service-flow policy was declared in advance; DocAble's upload-admission decision acquired its model in the opposite order, after a production failure exposed a representation that could no longer express the decision.
A user receives upload entitlement through groups — finite-credit or unlimited — so the admission decision depends on two facts: how many credits remain and whether any entitlement is unlimited.
The original credit comparison was understandable directly in code; unlimited entitlement made the policy harder to follow across implementation sites and motivated a separate decision model.
The finite-credit reduction excluded unlimited groups, while the client upload check ignored a separate unlimited-status signal and rejected the upload before the correct server gate was reached.

After fixing the client to read the existing unlimited signal, the team made the more complex entitlement policy explicit in a decision model and checked it with property tests, shared policy cases, and a shape check.

The revised model yields a structured admission decision and a separate display projection; unlimited use produces an admitting decision and a display sentinel, even though the group has zero finite credits.

The author changed the domain in one place and did not carry the change into every representation of the same decision; when the domain contains a consequential distinction, every representation used to reason about that decision must be capable of expressing it.

sections.heading_text: Connecting Models to Answer Engineering Questions
sections.topic_sentence: Connecting models lets us answer questions that no individual representation can settle.

points.text: Shared identities let different representations refer to the same service, work item, or operation without requiring a common file format or metamodel.
A static model and a history answer different questions; stable task identity permits a join when observations help answer a structural question.
An engineer or agent can begin at the entity named by a task and follow the modeled relationships required by its engineering question.
Joining models makes properties that cross individual representations available for reasoning.
A join can preserve entity identity while losing a distinction needed by the decision; shared identity does not establish semantic adequacy.

sections.topic_sentence: A connection remains useful only while the participating representations refer to the intended entities and preserve the relationships the analysis depends on.

points.text: Prefer shared identity and derivation over independently maintained copies of the same fact; where duplication is unavoidable, make the correspondence explicit and checkable.
Multiple models can diverge from the system or one another; the correspondence mechanism depends on which representation owns each fact.

Maintain correspondence according to the source of truth: derive a view from implementation, generate an artifact from a model or read the model during execution, or maintain traceability where neither side fully determines the other.

Where neither model nor implementation fully determines the other, traceability records a defined relationship between model elements and current implementation targets so engineers and agents can inspect correspondence and assess the impact of changes.
A runner can read a task model to determine dependency order and readiness without generating a separate artifact.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble uses connections among engineering models to answer questions about its remediation pipeline and deployed services.

points.text: DocAble's models differ in shape on purpose: roughly 130 structured model records plus data dialects share identities, derivations, query surfaces, and traceability where useful, are represented as data so map and territory stay separable, and nothing forces them into a single representation.

sections.heading_text: One Dependency for Execution and Analysis
sections.topic_sentence: Suppose we change a remediation pass.

points.text: The Office analytical graph projects resource edges from the same registry read/write metadata used by scheduling; the PDF projection uses parallel typed declarations held in correspondence by blocking checks.
One set of Office read/write declarations supplies both scheduling and analysis; PDF analytical relations instead depend on checked correspondence with parallel declarations.

sections.topic_sentence: A static computation graph does not record the mutations performed during a particular run.

points.text: Remediation-pass stamps and typed editor-session operations are distinct records whose selected grain supports audit, debugging, and derived history.
The applied-operation history and the lower-level PDF edit log are distinct; the replay engine applies supported pending edits, while both records omit the reasoning that produced them.

A typed changeset represents intended PDF mutations before application; per-operation results and attribution distinguish proposed changes from what was actually applied, independently of the producer's reasoning strategy.
Declared computations, recorded mutations, and replay answer what may compose, what happened in a run, and whether its recorded mutations can be reproduced.
Structural checks examine selected mutator populations for attribution wiring; they do not establish universal coverage or the semantic correctness of records.

sections.heading_text: Joining a Call to Its Deployment Permission
sections.topic_sentence: A permitted interservice call requires several models to agree.

points.text: The deployment dependency map joins to runtime identity and deployed service names to derive invocation grants; typed call declarations are checked against that map, and shared principals can collapse several logical callers into one binding.

preamble_points.text: Different questions require different models of one system; shared identity and explicit correspondence connect them where a question crosses views.
Externalize knowledge and intent into engineering models that both engineers and agents can reason through.

sections.topic_sentence: Guidance tells an agent what to do.

points.text: The environment intervenes between a proposed action and its consequence.
Guidance influences behavior; enforcement determines what the environment permits or accepts, and feedback returns evidence between them.
Recent agentic-security guidance draws a similar boundary: secure the process that produces the artifact.

sections.topic_sentence: [ref:2.6-system-knowledge:heading:maintaining-correspondence] examined several ways to maintain correspondence between a model and its implementation.

points.text: Drift checking has a precise job: preserve a declared correspondence between model and implementation; correctness needs another claim.
Three different relations matter — correspondence, conformance, or acceptance — and they are not interchangeable.
Enforcement needs an obligation independent of the work being judged, and a boundary at which that obligation is legible.
An obligation may live in a model, or directly in a type, permission, schema, test, or policy; Alignment does not require a particular representation.
A drift check establishes agreement between two artifacts, not that the correspondence expresses the right intent.
The distinction is not derived versus authored; it is description versus independent obligation.
Where an obligation permits variation, the acceptable region must come from governing intent, not from the realization being judged.

sections.topic_sentence: Chapter 2 distinguished descriptive models from models that are authoritative for a property.
Software testing has long confronted the *oracle problem*: how do we determine whether an observed result is correct?

points.text: Proofs and model checks evaluate stated properties under their assumptions; they do not establish that the chosen properties capture the engineering requirement.
Fix the required behavior before choosing an analysis; independence concerns the source of the obligation and the implementation judged against it.

sections.topic_sentence: Having established an obligation and decided what evidence would be adequate, how do we obtain that evidence from a changing implementation?

points.text: Requirements traceability connects intent, implementation, and evidence to support evaluation and change analysis.

Traceability can relate an obligation, its realization, and its evidence without any mechanism enforcing the obligation — a requirement can trace cleanly to a test whose failure is merely reported, and a permission boundary can enforce firmly without a rich traceability model.
Correspondence evidence is limited by what references and traces establish and by the operations they cover.

sections.topic_sentence: [ref:2.6-system-knowledge:heading:docable-connecting-engineering-models] described how I developed DocAble’s computation model by examining the computations and dependencies in its different document engines.

points.text: DocAble's execution machinery consumes a computation model, while an analytical view supports separate analysis and checks; the representation's governing role follows from its consumers.
Independent obligations and adequate evidence prepare the reader to choose enforcement mechanisms.

sections.topic_sentence: Return to the billing architecture: `Reporting` may obtain data through `BillingAPI`, but must not connect directly to `BillingDB`.

points.text: Constraints restrict possibilities, sensors produce evidence, and gates evaluate whether actions or results may proceed and enforce decisions. Checking may be advisory or used within a gate.
Constraints exclude particular actions or states; sensors supply evidence about behavior that remains possible.
The accompanying note connects constraints and feedback to systems-safety engineering without identifying agent engineering with a control system.
An instruction is enforced only when a mechanism in the environment acts on it.
A constraint excludes particular actions or representations within the scope of its language, interface, or runtime permissions; a closed type does not govern every possible behavior.
A sensor produces evidence about artifacts, attempted actions, or observed executions; observability exposes the state or behavior that the environment must inspect.
Evidence must preserve the distinctions needed to judge the obligation, such as caller identity, destination, and architectural component.
A gate evaluates whether an action or result may proceed, locally or through a delegated check, and enforces the decision; a blocking check can reject both genuine violations and false positives.
Instrumented tests produce observations, a checker compares them with the architectural model, and the merge gate requires the build and interaction checks to pass.
The merge gate uses build and interaction check results to decide whether a candidate meets its admission conditions.
Defense in depth combines protections with different coverage; tests and the gate that enforces their results constitute one protection together.

The Alignment Principle, stated whole: make engineering obligations enforceable by encoding them into mechanisms — constrain, sense, evaluate, admit — that can enforce them; an agent can misunderstand or forget an obligation while its enforcing mechanisms continue to operate.

sections.topic_sentence: Knowing a mechanism’s function does not establish that it enforces the intended obligation.
One way to preserve an engineering obligation is to restrict how an implementation can be constructed or changed.

points.text: In DocAble's PDF changeset interface, a closed operation vocabulary constrains proposals, the applier refuses unsupported targets or missing evidence, and subsequent validation checks selected properties of the resulting document.
A generator can embody selected obligations in implementation structure; this requires a valid model, a property-preserving transformation, and protection against bypass.

sections.topic_sentence: Recall the discussion of semantic commitment in [ref:2.2-constructing-and-using-engineering-models:heading:semantic-commitment-and-analysis].

points.text: Humans or agents may review an obligation, construct a bespoke check, or build reusable machinery that evaluates obligations expressed in a model.
Agents can construct checkers or controls for explicit obligations; generating a checker does not establish the checked implementation's correctness.

sections.topic_sentence: Tests can evaluate whether an implementation satisfies obligations expressed in a model.
Testing expected behavior is not enough when a system must also respond correctly to failures.
A passing test establishes that the implementation satisfied the checks performed.
Chapter 2 selected representations according to the engineering questions they could answer.

points.text: Generation, runtime constraints, tests, and model checking supply different kinds of restriction or evidence and can be combined for the obligation at hand.

sections.topic_sentence: Where practical, we can choose an operation that excludes a forbidden state rather than detect the state after it occurs.

points.text: An atomic conditional update can prevent competing claimants from both acquiring the same claim; tests and analysis can examine the surrounding protocol.

sections.topic_sentence: *Model checking* and *model-based testing* answer different questions.

points.text: Model checking explores the behavior admitted by an explicit model; model-based testing exercises an implementation against expected model behavior.
A universal eventuality claim requires reasoning about modeled executions and stated scheduling or recovery assumptions; a finite passing test does not establish it.
In DocAble, a lease makes abandoned work recoverable, while a separate durable claim restricts who may perform the protected effect; recovery alone does not supply that permission.

sections.topic_sentence: In the recovery protocol, I chose different verification techniques for different obligations.

sections.heading_text: Establishing That a Required Operation Occurred
sections.topic_sentence: We can sometimes protect an obligation more effectively by requiring an authorized operation than by trying to enumerate every forbidden alternative.

points.text: An admission mechanism may require reliable evidence that a protected operation passed through an authorized interface.
A gate can require evidence that a prescribed discovery procedure occurred; that evidence has limits distinct from whether the procedure was performed.

sections.topic_sentence: Choosing an enforcement mechanism also changes which implementation choices remain available.
Chapter 2 introduced tolerances as bounds on acceptable variation and degrees of freedom as choices left open to implementation.

points.text: Quantitative models define bounds; Alignment measures conformance and the remaining margin, making implementation freedom visible.

sections.topic_sentence: Alignment should preserve the implementation freedom that Modeling deliberately leaves open.

points.text: Controls can exclude alternatives that satisfy the stated obligations; cheap implementation makes more of those alternatives worth exploring.
Defer consequential commitments until the last responsible moment; cheap implementation changes the economics of waiting, and enforcement makes the deferral safer.
Obligations accept the region A, controls permit the region P; underconstraint is P minus A, overconstraint is A minus P.
Making the permitted region coincide with the acceptable one is an idealization; a deliberate restriction is legitimate — the point is a justified decision, not an accidental consequence.

sections.topic_sentence: Greater semantic commitment gives us more opportunities for mechanization, but we need not pursue all of them.

points.text: Where a goal lands turns on three questions; the first is whether the obligation is explicit in a form the environment can use.
The residual is an obligation nobody made explicit enough for the environment to use.
An explicit obligation may still resist cheap mechanical evaluation — an honest boundary, not failed Alignment.
Evaluated only: explicit and evaluated, but the result does not control whether work may proceed.
A governed obligation is enforced in a form appropriate to the engineering decision.
Making a tolerance explicit does not mean tightening it; stronger Alignment means dependable enforcement of the obligation engineers chose, not a narrower acceptable set.
An obligation can stop short of a gate for three different reasons; non-enforcement is sometimes the engineered result.

sections.topic_sentence: Where the environment intervenes determines what it can examine and control.

points.text: An obligation can be enforced at several boundaries; choose where it is visible and a mechanism can enforce it.
The first location is reasoning input: ordinarily guidance, not enforcement.
The first enforcement boundary is the action: one attempted side effect the harness can inspect or refuse.
The second enforcement boundary is the work unit, where whole-work obligations become legible.
The third enforcement boundary is the artifact or runtime: forbidden state made impossible to express or accept.

sections.heading_text: The Semantic Gap and Enforcement Placement
sections.topic_sentence: Which of these boundaries provides enough evidence?

points.text: An obligation can be stated clearly and still be unenforceable at the boundary where you try to check it.
Checking model drift at the commit is the wrong granularity; the property belongs to the completed unit of work.
Test the served page in a browser at the earliest boundary where the relevant composition can be exercised; a successful HTTP fetch alone does not establish correct rendering.
Place enforcement at the earliest boundary with sufficient evidence to evaluate the obligation and enforce the decision.
The rhyme: Modeling chooses the reduction that answers the question without carrying unnecessary detail; Alignment chooses the earliest boundary where the obligation is legible.

sections.topic_sentence: A later check is not necessarily a stronger check.

points.text: The four boundaries do not form a monotonic weak-to-strong scale.
Real boundaries are sometimes approximate: a hook that fires early enough to leave budget for the work beats the theoretically ideal hook.
Boundary placement affects what feedback can return and when; timely evidence lets an agent use the reasoning and context already at hand, while delayed feedback may require reconstruction.
These mechanisms do not act independently; the interplay is its own problem, deferred to §3.5.

sections.topic_sentence: The appropriate boundary depends on the obligation and the evidence needed to evaluate it.
Some engineering obligations are known before implementation begins.

points.text: Establish mechanisms for known obligations when violations are costly or evaluation recurs.

sections.topic_sentence: A failure may reveal that the engineering environment lacks something needed to guide or govern subsequent work.

points.text: Diagnose what was missing; not every failure calls for another gate.
The mechanism that discovers an obligation need not be the one that ultimately enforces it; Chapter 4 follows that migration.
A failure can expose missing representation, obligation, evidence, evaluation, or enforcement.
A correct validation result does not protect the system unless an appropriate mechanism acts on it.
A failure may require changes to models, sensors, evaluators, and enforcement mechanisms together; subsequent work uses the revised environment.

sections.topic_sentence: Governance conversion motivates a useful concept: **engineering capital**.

points.text: Governance conversion forms engineering capital — the concrete positive stock software engineering has lacked a name for.
Engineering capital consists of reusable models, checks, and other engineering machinery.
Capital earns a return: lower marginal engineering cost. Conversion is capital formation.
Engineering capital can transfer through reusable mechanisms or through the design judgment behind them; its value depends on work saved after adaptation and maintenance costs.
Inherited automation and principles improve a new project's starting conditions; they do not supply every representation or control the new system needs.
Capital depreciates; maintenance, reconciliation, and retirement manage it, so accumulation cannot be the objective.
Governance conversion creates a portfolio of controls that can themselves become inconsistent, redundant, or orphaned.

preamble_points.text: A governed environment grows from known obligations and engineering experience; governance conversion preserves lessons from failures in reusable models, procedures, and controls.

sections.topic_sentence: [ref:census-trio] illustrates three useful representations of the control machinery: a catalogue of the mechanisms, a graph of their interactions, and a view of their coverage of engineering obligations.

points.text: Catalogue each control: a stable identity, the boundary it acts at, the resources it touches, the obligation it serves, and its governance role.
A governance package can combine models, sensors, constraints, and gates with the checks used to evaluate evidence.
A collision lives between two controls, drawn nowhere until the graph draws it.

sections.topic_sentence: The interaction graph uses controls as nodes and shared resources as the principal join key.

points.text: The interaction graph uses controls as nodes and shared resources as the principal join key; controls need not call one another to collide.
Shared resource is a useful conservative relation, not a proof that the graph captured every interaction.
Some candidate conflicts are mechanically decidable; others require judgment about what the mechanisms demand.

Not every conflict between controls reflects a conflict between the obligations they enforce; incompatible obligations require revisiting requirements, while interfering mechanisms may be changed without weakening either obligation.

sections.topic_sentence: To find an uncovered obligation, start from the obligations engineers expect the environment to govern.

points.text: A catalogue says what exists and a graph says where controls collide; neither says what should be governed but is not.
Coverage is a small requirements-traceability problem: an obligation with no adequate mechanism is a coverage gap; a mechanism with no obligation is an orphan.
A coverage gap is an uncovered obligation; an orphan is a mechanism with no current purpose. Neither is automatically bad — an orphan is a finding to reconcile, not proof to delete.

sections.topic_sentence: In DocAble, I wanted to identify governance mechanisms that could interfere with one another.

points.text: DocAble adapts a classical read/write conflict test to identify potential access conflicts at a shared event; the governance model records resolutions and must also account for incompatible obligations.
Two turn-end hooks compete for a finite context budget. Their required order is recorded in the governance model, although the read/write conflict test does not discover it.

sections.topic_sentence: As we learn more about a system, we may introduce new controls.

points.text: New obligations and system changes motivate adding, revising, or retiring controls.
Entries in a control model identify the implementing mechanism, and correspondence checks expose missing or unrecognized targets instead of silently treating them as covered.
Extend the control model when an engineering question justifies its construction and maintenance.

preamble_points.text: Every control can be reasonable in isolation while the control machinery as a whole remains inconsistent, incomplete, or obsolete.
Governance conversion and up-front design accumulate control machinery; that machinery becomes an engineering object to maintain, reconcile, and sometimes retire.
Alignment turned on itself: a model of the controls, enforced on the controls.
Chapter 4 shows how engineers use and revise models and controls together as an engineering problem develops.

sections.topic_sentence: In Chapter 3, we examined how models and governance mechanisms can protect engineering obligations during implementation.
Chapter 2 organized models by the properties they represent.

sections.heading_text: Modeling Before, During, and After Implementation
sections.topic_sentence: In an existing system, we can recover models from the implementation.
Originally, one DocAble worker processed an entire document.
My first response was to introduce ChunkWorker, which divided a document into page ranges ([ref:interlude-execution-unit], panel b).
Dividing documents into page ranges reduced the amount of content each worker processed, but did not remove the underlying dependence on document size.
I introduced a representation that retained the document’s structure but kept its media elsewhere.
I intended to use the residency model to make decisions about worker memory allocations.

sections.heading_text: Memory as an Obligation for Subsequent Changes
sections.topic_sentence: I had prioritized memory because running out of it prevented DocAble from processing a document at all, whereas inefficient execution made processing slower or more expensive.
Skeletonization also gave me a reason to reconsider the execution architecture.

sections.heading_text: Using the Graph to Find and Remove Bottlenecks
sections.topic_sentence: More workers cost money.

sections.heading_text: Modeling the Cost of Repeated Document Processing
sections.topic_sentence: Improving the GenAI operations was an obvious way to try to reduce latency.
Running more computations concurrently in the cloud would introduce overhead for starting workers, transferring information, and coordinating their work.

sections.heading_text: Evaluating a Design Before Implementing It
sections.topic_sentence: Implementing an architectural alternative merely to discover that it would be too slow is an expensive way to evaluate a design.
I was using these predictions to decide which designs were worth implementing.
The memory model also made predictions that I could test independently of the implementation’s apparent success.
As I developed these models, I had to decide which of their properties should constrain subsequent engineering.

sections.heading_text: Combining Models to Answer Engineering Questions
sections.topic_sentence: I could no longer make decisions about concurrency by considering latency alone.

sections.heading_text: Using the Models to Evaluate Subsequent Changes
sections.topic_sentence: The models developed during this episode also helped me reason about changes I had not yet undertaken.
In §4.2, I constructed models to answer new engineering questions about DocAble.
We can recover models from several sources.
As DocAble grew, I became concerned that some important domain concepts remained implicit in its implementation.
Recovering a model need not immediately lead to changes in the implementation.
Recall the distinction between correspondence and conformance introduced in [ref:3.1-from-engineering-models-to-enforcement:heading:agreement-is-not-correctness].

sections.heading_text: Introducing Enforcement into an Existing System
sections.topic_sentence: When introducing new checks into DocAble, I often used a three-stage procedure: Audit, Drain, Promote.
A method has to survive terrible, horrible, no good, very bad days, too.

points.text: A validation bottleneck prompted independent scheduling of broad checks, with cheap checks before merge and full validation before deployment; the redesign traded detection delay and attribution cost against integration cost.

sections.heading_text: Improving the Execution of Engineering Work
sections.topic_sentence: As I increased the number of agents developing DocAble, the engineering environment encountered resource problems of its own.
An audit of my engineering models appeared to show that ten providers had the required uniqueness checks.

sections.heading_text: What Does a Software Factory Produce?
sections.topic_sentence: The analogy requires one adjustment before we apply it to software.

points.text: Software is readily copied, while a software service may be one continuously evolving system.
The output of a software factory is the next working realization of an evolving product.
A software factory preserves consequential properties while changing the system itself.
A software factory organizes controlled change while preserving control over consequential properties and consequences.
Representations of changing software incur construction and maintenance costs.
Organizations weigh reusable representations against the cost of skilled judgment during implementation.
The economic question is where consequential knowledge can be maintained and applied most economically without losing control.
Engineers can preserve selected consequential judgments while leaving agents substantial implementation freedom.

sections.topic_sentence: If we are to adopt the metaphor of a software factory, we must consider how such factories might be organized.

points.text: Four questions guide comparison: what the factory produces, what people do, how production is organized, and which product tolerances must be satisfied.
A longitudinal case explains development and mechanisms, while public industrial accounts expose variation in the allocation of work, authority, and control.

preamble_points.text: The printer analogy explained fabricative technology — a machine that realizes a broad range of artifacts from a description of what should be made.

The printer metaphor expands rather than being replaced: once fabrication becomes a means of production, the fabricator sits inside a larger system that decides what should be made, organizes production, and judges what is acceptable.

Interchangeable parts, mechanization, and machine tools each made production more repeatable and each exposed a problem, so scaling fabrication required engineering the production system around the fabricator.
Two techniques from that history carry into software factories: process design determines how production proceeds, and tolerance states which variation in the product is acceptable.
Watt's engine needed cylinders more accurately bored than ordinary production could manage; Wilkinson's machinery made the design practical, connecting production capability to product tolerance.

sections.topic_sentence: In 2024, the U.S.

points.text: The 2024 DOJ rule set WCAG 2.1 AA and a 2026 deadline; four days before the deadline, the Department extended it by a year.
The requirements were ordinary production-software requirements; the unusual condition was one engineer’s implementation capacity.
The eight requirements briefly introduced in §1.3 are stated in full here as the requirements that guided DocAble’s development.

Production use required preservation, reviewable changes, standards-grounded evaluation, and dependable operation alongside semantic reasoning; these obligations shaped the product and its engineering environment.

sections.topic_sentence: I tested the uncertain capability first.

points.text: The probe supplied initial evidence of semantic reasoning on equations, technical slides and handwritten notes.

The initial semantic capability supported building a remediation system around the foundation model; preservation, reviewability, conformance, dependable operation, and practical cost remained engineering obligations.

sections.heading_text: The Two Rules of Agentic Software Engineering
sections.topic_sentence: I began with two rules.

points.text: Not reading the code was deliberate: inspecting agent-produced implementation would have bounded implementation throughput by the engineer's own reading capacity, so the first rule made reading the last resort and an engineering environment the surface through which work was directed and judged.

The rule did not forbid reading source: needing to read it pointed to a missing supervisory surface — a model, test, lint, instrument, or architectural boundary — so reading was the escape hatch, not the operating model.

The second rule required the resulting system to be good, fast, and cheap — partly a DocAble requirement, partly a test of whether agents could help build a production system good enough to trust, fast enough to matter, and cheap enough to deploy at scale.

A fast factory producing poor software would fail the test, and so would a high-quality system that stayed prohibitively expensive to develop or operate; agentic implementation was valuable only if the engineering system around it achieved all three.

sections.topic_sentence: DocAble’s development began with PowerPoint remediation, then expanded to Word, Excel, and PDF as colleagues brought other documents (R1).

points.text: Format expansion, deployment, user failures and changed deadline pressure drove successive development stages.

sections.topic_sentence: As I built DocAble, I also built the machinery for building it.

points.text: The 31-week repository reconstruction preserves landed commits, model/check inventories, dispatches and documented Epic completions as distinct measures.
Work commits exclude duplicates and bookkeeping; Epic completions count recorded claims; model paths account for changes in declaration conventions.
Models and registered verifier files accumulated; the inventories establish available structure rather than successful execution.
Week 11 field notes and commit topics support a transition toward durable deterministic checks; first surviving records do not date the origin of the practices.

sections.topic_sentence: The source composition gives a different view of the investment ([ref:support-ratio-curve]).

points.text: Ten consistently categorized snapshots show the growing apparatus; support ratio measures investment rather than return.
The exhibits show accumulated implementation and structure, leaving project feasibility as an author’s engineering judgment.

sections.topic_sentence: The supporting apparatus recorded in [ref:support-ratio-curve] includes models of service workflows, state ownership, and resource bounds, together with their consumers.

points.text: Models of workflows, ownership, and resource bounds connect to consumers that supply context, derive configuration, and check obligations.

sections.topic_sentence: The 31-week reconstruction identifies 143 model modules at the final snapshot.

points.text: The 31-week reconstruction identifies 143 model modules; models remain maintained artifacts rather than a fixed inventory.

Six specimens show the models' purpose: each representation answers an engineering question for a consumer, and its supervisory consequence is what the engineer no longer reconstructs from implementation.

sections.heading_text: The Joins: Deriving Evidence and Enforcement
sections.topic_sentence: In [ref:chapter:2.6-system-knowledge], we saw how connections among models help engineers answer questions about a system.

points.text: Connections among models determine required verification, access-grant plans, and recorded evidence, reducing repeated engineering decisions.
Modeled property facts determine the required verification artifact; a reusable gate checks its existence without establishing that verification has been performed.
Service relationships, deployment wiring, and runtime identities determine an access-grant plan; the resulting grants still require evaluation.
A common provenance mechanism supports derived changelogs and checks selected mutation paths for required attribution or justified exemptions.

sections.heading_text: Computation Declarations Shared by Execution and Analysis
sections.topic_sentence: The computation model introduced in [ref:2.3-structural:heading:what-computations-depend-on-one-another] became reusable infrastructure within DocAble's factory.

points.text: Typed pass declarations determine dependency order and remain connected to analytical views by correspondence checks.

sections.topic_sentence: The factory’s accumulated models, tools, and controls helped preserve a separation within DocAble’s architecture: the reasoning that proposes document repairs is distinct from the machinery that applies and evaluates them.

points.text: Task-level foundation-model selection and experimental agent orchestration change different parts of DocAble's reasoning while reusing supported document operations; the common PDF changeset interface does not cover every remediation pass.
Selecting a foundation model was itself an engineering decision: frontier foundation models were reserved for judgments where their additional capability earned their additional cost.
Prepared representations can reduce what a foundation model reconstructs, but the reported scaffold and agent experiments used different fixtures.
A September 2026 single-PDF comparison measured pipeline inference at $0.0419 and estimated agent execution at $2.29; accounting and reference exposure limit the comparison.
A November 2026 two-PDF repair-loop evaluation closed no additional findings; the harder document cost $3.57 versus $1.35, so the loop was not promoted.

sections.topic_sentence: How does one engineer keep several agents working without continually prompting each one?

points.text: The November 3 workflow turns priorities into reviewed work orders, dependency-ordered phases, isolated implementation and independently audited completion.
An agent's refined target files let Query Repo retrieve relevant models, invariants, tests, and analyses before implementation; a separate check requires that discovery occurred.
Checks and the completion audit return deficient work for repair; unresolved decisions and defects in the environment reach the engineer.

sections.topic_sentence: The factory’s operating process also exposed failures that required changes to the factory itself.

points.text: Three selected episodes show a controlled product interface, evidence-grounding prompt checks, and integration policy becoming durable machinery.

sections.topic_sentence: As DocAble’s engineering environment developed, my role changed with it.

points.text: Three supervisory stages summarize how accumulated GEE capability supported more abstract supervision, not a prescribed maturity model.

preamble_points.text: Earlier chapters teach product decisions and governing mechanisms; this section examines the factory through which one engineer directed coding agents.
DocAble's governed engineering environment was part of a factory that also included people, agents, processes, and arrangements governing engineering decisions.
Goals, users, production failures, standards and institutional use supplied engineering work; the engineer made consequential decisions while coding agents wrote every implementation line.
Process design organized work and tolerance preserved consequential requirements while agents retained implementation freedom; failures could require changes to both the product and its factory.

The case follows factory development from initial requirements through production operation; implementation, institutional use, and observed failures exposed engineering decisions that needed to persist.

sections.topic_sentence: **Human reference.** Across approximately six months, 42 trained undergraduates remediated documents.

points.text: The trained undergraduate corpus provides artifacts and billed labor for a reference workflow, not expert ground truth or matched labor savings.
The agent baseline uses separate configurations and a ten-document cohort; results compare automatic findings, runtime, and inference expenditure.
The human-reference evaluation separately measures checker findings and transcript-based semantic improvements relative to the original.
DocAble led on PDF and DOCX median checker reductions; humans led on PPTX. Of 62 rubric scores, 20 favored DocAble, 41 fell in parity, and one favored the human output.
A title-only description passed a checker but omitted table contents; a transcription improved access to those contents, while other examples favored human repair.
Fallible transcript assessment, inconclusive criteria, changed checkers and unmeasured visual and screen-reader properties limit the results.

sections.topic_sentence: **Runtime and inference cost.** Median elapsed time across all 63 attempts, including the failed attempt, was 1.36 minutes.

points.text: The 63 attempts had median runtime 1.36 minutes; 62 completed outputs had median inference cost $0.066, excluding unmeasured review and full cloud costs.
Operating the product, building the product and factory, and changing the product incur distinct costs.
Measured inference expenditure, estimated development investment, and observed change capacity establish different things; per-change cost remains unmeasured.

sections.topic_sentence: The case follows one primary engineer directing multiple coding agents within one contemporary model ecosystem, without a controlled comparison against another engineering process.

points.text: The evidence has clear limits: one longitudinal case, one primary engineer, one model ecosystem, no controlled comparison — the case establishes mechanism and sequence, not prevalence.
DocAble illustrates one response to increased implementation capacity; other organizations begin with different resources and constraints.

preamble_points.text: The evaluation distinguishes remediation comparisons, production economics, and the limits of a longitudinal case.

sections.topic_sentence: Cloudflare operates a global network that provides security, performance, and connectivity services for Internet applications.

points.text: Cloudflare represents institutional obligations as individually identified statements that can be tracked through revision and applied at several stages of engineering work.
Standards approval and enforcement promotion are separate; enforced MUST statements can drive merge decisions, with a recorded human override.
Operating experience changed the representation of extracted standards and moved suitable checks into deterministic linters; engineering knowledge becomes more usable and cheaper to enforce.

sections.topic_sentence: Spotify operates a music and audio streaming service supported by many independently developed software components.

points.text: Spotify introduced agents into a pre-existing fleet-change process, reusing its production and verification machinery.
Bounded tools and mandatory checks govern proposed changes; an added judge and its reported later removal show controls changing with observed failures and false vetoes.
People set migration scope, maintain prompts, reserve judgment calls, and review agent-authored changes; delegation varies within the production process.
Rework, complexity, pull-request size, and incident observations provide a mixed account of system health and verification capacity rather than an activity-only success claim.

sections.topic_sentence: Shopify develops a commerce platform through which merchants operate online stores, manage transactions, and run their businesses.

points.text: Public River sessions let colleagues inspect work and failures and record useful knowledge for subsequent sessions.
People record missing knowledge in shared files; the reported merge-rate improvement occurred with the foundation model held fixed.
Shared instructions require upkeep when different agent tools consume different files; repairing that divergence is part of maintaining the engineering environment.
A failed enumeration requirement motivates code enforcement of closure rules; the security workflow retains human merge authority, fresh evidence, and post-merge verification.

sections.topic_sentence: Uber operates a platform for transportation and delivery, supported by software services that coordinate users, providers, transactions, and real-time operations.

points.text: Uber treats foundation-model choice, context, orchestration, workflow cost, and reviewer attention as measurable engineering variables.
Uber describes producer-assembled evidence followed by additional review, CI, and human approval, while exploring partial automatic approval.
Review latency exposes finite reviewer capacity; rising fabrication capacity increases demands on supervision and the surrounding production process.
Context delivery, orchestration, foundation-model selection, and outcome-denominated costs make the agent's surrounding production system an object of optimization.

sections.topic_sentence: Amazon develops software for commerce and cloud computing, including Amazon Web Services (AWS), whose products depend on large, continuously evolving software systems.

points.text: Kiro supplies a reviewable specification workflow that adopting teams connect to their own repositories, tools, and engineering decisions.
Property-based tests provide evidence and configured hooks can enforce selected conditions; coverage and blocking decisions remain project responsibilities.

Bedrock's reported use combined Kiro with scoped work, tests, operational tools, and senior review; the twentyfold figure measures normalized commit velocity rather than quality or isolated causal effect.
Kiro-trace tests proposed harness changes against an unchanged control and regression requirements, with human merge decisions and new checks derived from evaluation failures.

sections.topic_sentence: GitLab develops a software-development platform that brings source control, code review, continuous integration, and deployment workflows into a common environment.

points.text: GitLab integrates organizational context with CI and permission boundaries, including a security-review flow that cannot approve changes.

sections.topic_sentence: Siemens develops industrial technologies and engineering software used to design, simulate, manufacture, and maintain physical products.

sections.heading_text: What the Factories Share, and Where They Differ
sections.topic_sentence: The factories differ in the products they support, the work they delegate, and the engineering machinery through which they govern production.

points.text: The cases reveal distinct allocations of production and acceptance authority and distinct arrangements for supervisory capacity and engineering knowledge.
Production and supervisory capacity can grow at different rates; review delays, workload scheduling, and verification experience make this a process-design concern.

Standards, observed agent work, supplied specification workflows, measured experiments, and construction failures provide different routes for preserving engineering knowledge beyond an individual task.
Shared knowledge and checks require maintenance; the documented revisions show how reusable engineering structure exchanges repeated judgment for upkeep.

preamble_points.text: The longitudinal DocAble case is compared with organizations possessing different teams, processes, institutional knowledge and obligations; the four factory questions organize the comparison.
Public reports, talks, and documentation provide seven independently developed arrangements interpreted through the four factory questions.
DocAble developed production arrangements as implementation outpaced individual supervision; established organizations adapted existing engineering processes, representations, analyses, and controls.
Human incentives and accountability remain distinct from agent capability; engineering authority determines delegation and controls, and the theory chapter examines their costs and effects.

sections.heading_text: Did We Build What We Intended?
sections.topic_sentence: Let us begin with a single engineering task that an engineer chooses to delegate to an agent.

points.text: The encoding–realization decomposition applies the chain rule to distinguish adequate encoding from fulfillment, before extending the account to delivery cost and accumulated structure.

The probabilities belong to a production system: the factory of Chapter 5, redrawn with each step of the realization path carrying the probability that it succeeds and the encoded property also supplying the tolerance the result is evaluated against.

sections.topic_sentence: The first term is easy to overlook in an agentic setting.

points.text: A representation can improve P(E
Feedback from a failed realization can help diagnose an encoding problem; capable agents may improve encoding indirectly when that diagnosis supports revising intent.
Process design changes the conditions and cost of realization. Explicit tolerances help encode intent and make selected properties available for independent evaluation.
Better reasoners may reconstruct meaning from a weak representation, but some lost distinctions require a different representation or additional evidence.
With encoding quality fixed, perfectly reliable fulfillment leaves faithful production bounded by the encoding term; this does not imply complete specification.
Useful freedom lets agents choose satisfactory realizations while engineers specify consequential obligations; complete specification is not the objective.

sections.topic_sentence: Having considered whether an agent produces the intended result, we turn to what it costs.

points.text: Cost per correct admitted change counts construction, all attempts and upkeep over comparable requested work and a declared horizon.
Comparable requested work, quality and horizon prevent an attractive cost ratio from concealing rejected or unfinished work.

sections.heading_text: The Cost of Production and Assurance.
sections.topic_sentence: Admission adds the cost of gathering evidence and acting on it.

points.text: Validation, false rejection, and repair consume running cost even when the admission mechanism’s protection stays unchanged.
Human review and intervention consume engineering resources even when machine execution is inexpensive.
Human attention is an engineering resource.

sections.topic_sentence: Should we keep the knowledge explicit or pay to figure out the same thing again?

points.text: A representation earns its construction and upkeep through useful work enabled or later costs avoided, compared with inference over less explicit knowledge.
A packaged agent system may substitute capable inference and generic machinery for some explicit structure; compare what it delivers, costs, and leaves for later work.
Lifecycle accounting supports comparison; choosing reasoning, representation and assurance is a constrained engineering decision.

sections.heading_text: How Does Today’s Work Affect Tomorrow’s?
sections.topic_sentence: The cost of one engineering change is not the whole story.

points.text: Models, controls and architectural changes affect the reliability and cost of later work.
Faithful production depends schematically on the task, foundation model, and available GEE; an episode can change that GEE without necessarily improving it.
Agentic capacity and the available GEE jointly shape what the factory can accomplish; experience can change the GEE and affect later production.
Corrective feedback requires structural diagnosis and authority to adapt the GEE; the resulting changes affect subsequent work.
Useful representations, adequate coverage, coherence and economy describe GEE fit independently of machinery counts.

sections.topic_sentence: The dynamic model raises a practical question: which changes to the GEE actually improve subsequent engineering?

points.text: The properties are dimensions for diagnosing what limits the work, not maturity stages; the appropriate response may improve representations or assurance, or reconcile and retire controls.
Durable throughput, defect escape and human-attention burden are outcomes; their candidate observables require explicit measurement choices.

sections.topic_sentence: The dynamic model distinguishes the engineering environment from the results it produces.

points.text: Easy-to-count quantities (commits, lines, control files, support ratio) measure activity or investment, not outcome.
The schematic descriptions motivate four conditional propositions about useful progress, but supply no measured effect sizes.

preamble_points.text: Chapter 5 examined the complete software factory; the theory focuses on its GEE and how reusable engineering structure supports the encoding and realization of intent.

sections.topic_sentence: *Proposition 1.

points.text: Trustworthy task-relevant representations can reduce reconstruction and extend reasoning reach at matched quality and resources, when their value justifies construction and upkeep.

sections.topic_sentence: Consider an agent asked to remediate a large document.

points.text: DocAble’s large-document representation exposes the choice between purchasing more context and reducing what each judgment requires.
DocAble’s HTML/CSS export was estimated at roughly 590,000 tokens against a 272,000-token context; windowing and compression reduced the information required for each judgment.
A representation can change the reasoning required, a mechanism established in external-representation research and applied here to maintained engineering models.
A useful model can preserve earlier reasoning so that later work begins with the consequential structure, while remaining bounded by its coverage.

sections.topic_sentence: The proposition does not require engineers to design every representation in advance.

points.text: Representations can be designed, recovered from existing systems, or invented to expose previously impractical relationships; each requires validation for its claimed use.
Discovery does not confer trust: a machine-proposed representation still must earn trust in the relationship it claims.
Representation leverage is challenged when apparent gains disappear at matched quality/resources or construction, interpretation and upkeep erase them.

sections.topic_sentence: *Proposition 2.

points.text: Representations can make selected obligations mechanically decidable, while Alignment enforces them independently of producer compliance.

sections.topic_sentence: Suppose an architectural rule forbids a service from depending on a database directly.

points.text: A dependency model guides production; an independent gate governs which results are admitted, whether or not the producer consulted the model.
A sound mechanism excludes its covered failure class; practical assurance must also account for scope, false rejection, missed failures and wrong obligations.

sections.topic_sentence: Modeling can change which obligations admit such mechanisms.

points.text: A representation can expose the relation that a repeatable predicate needs, reducing per-instance semantic reconstruction for a covered obligation.

The determinization frontier separates judgment supplied per instance from judgment the environment can carry repeatably — in factory terms, an economic boundary between judgments still bought probabilistically through the production process and properties made durable as tolerances.
Some judgments yield checkable properties while others remain semantic; the determinization frontier moves through representation and adequate evidence, not assertion.

sections.heading_text: Proposition 3: Governance Conversion and Engineering Capital (P3)
sections.topic_sentence: *Proposition 3.
